If you have any experience with Richii Mahjong, then it's pretty hard to find a challenging or engaging experience. Score multipliers are way too high, you're flooded with items and currency to make progress even easier, and the discards are incredibly generous. Even with a string of bad-luck, you'll be hard-pressed to struggle. This game also becomes a slog about halfway through a run, failing to duplicate Balatro's snappy game-play loop. There are 16 rounds, with a boss encounter every 8; but it's pretty simple to just beat the target score in a few hands and progress. This game is in Early Access, so maybe it will improve with enough time. But at the moment, I would recommend Ultimahjong over this one; Ultimahjong is a much cleaner game with a more engaging and challenging gameplay loop.

如果有更细致的评价其实我会选择更细的，但是基于只有好评不评和差评，我感觉还是选择一下差评好点 小丑牌like的麻将，一开始就注定了不得不和小丑牌比较 麻将虽然更具有东亚风格，但是和扑克比肉鸽内容天生就有一个基本的问题，卡组厚度远大于传统的卡组构筑类rouge，在这个基础上策划的选择是给了玩家更多的卡牌删除的道具，但是依旧改变不了这个游戏的删卡相关操作很糟心，百来张卡里面去roll8张，之后花需要阶梯价格的钱删除，随着卡组变薄价格甚至飞升，导致80卡之后的删卡基本上需要使用道具，而道具要求打出，为了删卡去选择的遗物也基本上都是非常局限，如果我在后续的数值膨胀中能轻松的打出我还考虑删了这卡干嘛？ 其次是养成问题（最关键但是因为槽点太多了我放第二点说），传统的肉鸽的养成路子里基本上是深度挖掘的，即选择路线之后在这个路线下继续选择更适合自己的内容继续调整结构。但是你们的内容呢，基本上套路方面的成长线只有两三个遗物就决定了，后续的倍率遗物基本上为了数值可选的很少，甚至为了这些数值我需要去放弃当前的牌型来凹别的牌型才能达到高倍率，这种东西对于别的肉鸽而言是少量并且变化要求没那么大的，但是这游戏的呢，摧毁掉当前宝牌，激活没激活过的紫色以上牌型，镜面顺子，两种以下役种……基本上要么是完全两个流派的，要么是需要多个遗物或稀有道具配合的，这还只是遗物上，牌面上的数值维度更是神奇，牌面本身提升的遗物，条子牌面翻倍遗物（竹酒），牌身，颜色，宝牌……以至于这个游戏你想拿到高牌需要进行非常多的处理流程，才能拿到一个数值高一点的牌（最大牌面需要七条先用其他遗物叠到400，之后用翻倍遗物触发十三次，这样才能得到一个400万的牌面，为了更高番的胡牌牌型还需要变成白板，之后用稀有道具变牌面成万，再之后用另个稀有道具三分之一概率变成白板，再使用另个道具固定，这样才能得到一个大牌，后续虽然能用道具复制，但是这个流程要多久，游戏的分数膨胀又多快？）这样得到的理论上最大牌型有多少分呢？10的50次方，基本上这游戏不可能比这个大了，但是过不了百关，你还用了大量的时间去凹和刷新，这就是数值体验吗？你是觉得你的马赛克动画放大缩小有节奏还是你的积分成长没关卡爬升快有快感？就这样策划还想着盯着数值平衡不放，你一个单机肉鸽玩家后期 至于关卡boss，更是一大坨。关卡本身流程短，基本上玩家要过高难就是刷道具或者强行堆数值，基本上没build体验，因为没build就死了或者过了。boss瞄准特定套路的设计到底是谁，盯着流派打的设计简直是一坨大粪，污染手牌的（并且污染保留会在后续游戏继续污染牌库），有颜色就长番的（我玩红一色是不是就不用玩了？），有高品质道具就会降低获得的分数的（为了过关需要卖掉成长类遗物），需要连打两次的（小牌库打完一次够你抗第二次？）简直就是指着玩家的构筑说你的套路在我机制面前一坨，重新做一个或者自认倒霉，啥，你说为什么不能根据boss情报提前调整？boss情报方面，提过意见，但是策划好像觉得“上半场能看到上半场的两个boss，下半场能看到下半场的两个boss是个好设计”，毕竟这游戏的奇数轮boss的强度和内容恶心人的也不少，就是后续有一坨屎我也要给你先藏着，快到了再给你来个jumpscare，因为奇数轮boss导致无尽堆数值失败的局体验感一团糟，但是出于这个游戏的策划特别喜欢数值平衡和凹数值，但这个问题和上面说的别的比就没那么大了 至于你说为什么我玩了那么久还来差评，是不是爽了就丢了，这是肉鸽卡牌，两小时谁打得完，几十小时当入门真的正常（虽然这游戏撑不起那么久，但是毕竟不花时间凹和碰运气就是过不去，成就癌），这个制作组唯一选对的地方就是选了这个类型，毕竟这样他们的奇思妙想奥利给藏在后面你吃了也退不了款，阳谋，真的阳谋 故此，差评，这个组和发行商（眼光不行）我个人就不推荐了，想买的快跑

There are things about Aotenjo I like, and things about it I really don't like, and they're sort of battling in my head. I think what it comes down to is this game is just really not for me, because I can't help but play it and feel like i'm not really getting the "mahjong experience" at all. Understandably things need to be changed for it to work as a single player roguelite experience... but as I played through a couple runs it felt like when the developers hit the fork in the road of "keep it like mahjong" vs "make it into something different", they chose the latter almost every single time. Firstly, it's single player with no opponents. That's fine, and something I totally expected- making a mahjong AI that can also calculate/deal with all the weird roguelite stuff going on at the same time sounds like a nightmare to balance. You would spend years on something like that and have to sacrifice a lot of the game's quirks to make it work properly. The bigger thing that I struggle to get over is the fact that you build your hand one set at a time, along with a pair. The pair is especially odd because it makes you play 6 more tiles than what you would in a mahjong hand- in a lot of cases this makes forming good hands harder because you have to find pairs to play all the time. What's even weirder is that you can "skip" some of these turns to gain more discards, meaning your final hand could end up being 11, 8, or even 5 tiles large. In combination with playing your hands in 1-4 "steps" which score individually, this makes Aotenjo feel a lot less like mahjong and a lot more like playing 4 poker hands that always require one pair. The yaku are also pushed to the top of the UI and calculated during each of these four rounds, rather than the traditional "round end results screens" most online mahjong games employ. At one point I won a round by just playing [1, 2, 3][7, 7] of characters, it was then that I really had to ask myself if anything I was doing felt like mahjong at all. After playing outside of tutorial mode once, I ended up purely going for seven pairs and thirteen orphans to try and get this single-turn-gambling-rush back, but it quickly turned stale considering it's only two types of hands. I complain a lot about this, but I also think that it enables some fun strategies for people who are more open to this idea. Since your "total hand" scores up to four times, you ideally want to play your strongest tiles in your first play, since they get scored the maximum amount of times. I think the items are fairly unique and especially enjoyed one that ended up painting all my tiles to be aka dora. The single use consumables are fun and thematic, such as taping over the number on a character tile to increment its number by one. Making up new yaku that can only exist in a roguelite is something that made me say "hell yeah" out loud when I got my first one, I enjoyed getting silly things like "six of one tile"! Finally, the shop variety was pretty enjoyable, and even if it was confusing at first I liked having to decide between what types of shops I wanted to go to (but it needs some sort of visual aid to make choices quicker). Generally, I found everything surrounding the core gameplay of Aotenjo to be interesting and worth expanding upon, I just can't get past how the game fundamentally works. It almost feels like you could reskin the game to just be a standard deck of cards and it wouldn't feel too out of place. I understand a lot of the concessions that were made to make the game not frustrating for players... if you had to form your hand all at once, what would happen if you didn't have a legal hand at the end? Would you just lose? It would be a lot trickier to wrangle together the balance with a lot less design space, but I almost wish they went balls to the wall and attempted to figure it out. There could have been a bigger focus on discarding rather than playing, potentially scoring fu/triggering effects on things you discard, etc. But i'm getting off topic now... at the end of the day I just don't think it's for me. I'm not sure if "mahjong balatro" can ever exist without sacrificing large chunks of riichi mahjong, but to me Aotenjo feels like it cuts so much out that the original game is barely recognisable. EDIT: After reviewing this I tried out the demo for Ultimahjong, which was much closer to what I wanted from a mahjong roguelite (and understandably a million times less approachable). Not sure how it'll shape out since it's not even out in early access yet, but if you felt similar to how I did after playing Aotenjo just thought i'd mention there are other options potentially coming in the future! EDIT EDIT: Ultimahjong has ceased development at the time of writing this, I still encourage playing the demo if it sounds interesting- I also have listed some other gimmicky mahjong games in the comments if you're interested in more

I've played a ton of various Mahjong games and play Riichi fairly regularly. This game is not for people with experience playing Mahjong. With 60 hours playtime at the time of writing, I can say without a doubt that this game is far too chance based. While there are absolutely strategies that are somewhat consistent this game relies way too heavily on random chance, particularly at the higher difficulty levels; a run can be decided entirely by what shows up at any given time. Very rarely does a run come down to skill and planning. While I cannot deny that the game is fun, it is frequently extremely frustrating. Even good compositions with decent artifacts can be completely crushed by bad draws. It also doesn't help that every balance patch has made more and more strategies less viable. Unless this game gets a complete overhaul, I cannot suggest it. Additionally, many reviews mention that this game is similar to Balatro, and while that is true, there is way more variety in this game, which, I believe, is to its detriment.

本质上是小丑牌的换皮，但实际玩起来各方面比小丑牌要差很多。如果小丑牌能打10分的话，这个游戏目前来看最多打个6分。 1、牌型过于复杂。我一个线下重度麻瘾少年+线上雀魂600+小时，竟然根本记不住这游戏里这么多牌型。记不住牌型带来的后果就是，算分根本算不明白。赢得稀里糊涂，输的不明不白。 2、游戏里各种术语晦涩难懂。名字我就不说了（因为根本记不住），反正作者就是凭空发明出来了很多词。小丑牌里出现的很多词汇，其实是现实中存在的。比如把「关卡」换成了「盲注」，塔罗牌这种东西也是大家耳熟能详的。更不要说，小丑牌的名字本身就有很多有趣好玩的彩蛋。但这款游戏里的很多词汇，我感觉就是嗯编出来的。咱要不试试用AI生成一下呢？ 3、界面UI实在是太粗糙了。这个要重点说一下，玩过这个游戏，我才意识到，刨除优秀的玩法，小丑牌UI的精美真的是被大大忽略了。界面简洁，主次分明，区域划分清晰，让人很容易入门上手。反观这款游戏，甚至连最基本的主次都没有分清楚。很多使用频次高，且作用重要的按钮做的完全不够醒目。每一关通关之后的界面，一大堆东西贴满屏幕，根本让人无所适从，不知道点哪里。另外就是这款游戏的字体也比较难绷。实在不行换微软雅黑我也是能接受的…… 优点还是有的：1、麻将碰撞的声音我好喜欢哈哈哈，解压又治愈。2、玩法本身确实足够有亮点（小丑牌的含金量还在提升）3、作者还在不停地更新。冲这点，给个推荐吧。 上班摸鱼也不错的~

Context: I'm a fairly novice mahjong player with some experience in Cantonese and have read Dana Chiba's riichi books. This game is different enough from actual mahjong to be somewhat frustrating (eg playing sets sequentially, each with a pair, rather than playing a fully-formed hand all at once, and no defensive play because you're playing against score targets rather than simulated opponents). Each run is very long, and it takes a lot to unlock new variants (though this has improved recently). It often feels like there are too many variant mechanics all happening at once - tiles have color and material (which you are usually trying to improve), and gadgets let you modify them during a single round, and patterns vary their point values based on choices you've made, and you have the ability to remove tiles from your wall (or set them up for later removal with fracture), and then relics interact with all of these things, and then "bosses" have mechanics where you have limited foresight and which are sometimes no-ops and sometimes run-killers depending on what you've been doing. And that's all in the basic, initial version of the game; later more stuff opens up (with eg dora). It feels unfocused, scattershot. I think a game mode primarily focused on improving tile materials and wall composition, another focused primarily on gadgets and patterns, and a third focused on colors might have been a better design. This would also allow boss mechanic pools to be restricted to ones that interact with that theme, preventing no-op bosses (if bosses must be kept at all). A more charitable way of putting this might be: there are at least three or four interesting mahjong-for-score variation games in here, but they're all stepping on each others' toes all the time. Less might be more. This wild complexity is compounded by unclear relic and boss mechanic descriptions. Sometimes I can't tell what a boss' mechanics will do until after I've played my first set and seen it happen. Then when I lose to a boss mechanic I didn't understand from the text, it will be several hours until I see it again. Likewise, I have bought relics only to realize after a round or two that I completely misunderstood their terse descriptions. Overall I've found Aotenjo more frustrating than fun, but it has promise; I'll check back on it when it exits Early Access.

A full year after release, Aotenjo is still something I'd have a hard time recommending to most people. It's not necessarily a bad game, but it proves that the Balatro format doesn't work well with mahjong and has a bit of an issue with scope creep. Balatro worked because the rules of poker are universal: no matter which deck you pick, you're playing using the same rules and most of the hands (barring the Flush House and Flush Five) exist in actual poker. In Aotenjo, some decks use a ruleset loosely based on Japanese mahjong while others use a ruleset loosely based on Chinese mahjong, which forces you to memorize two different sets of base yaku. Because getting a valid hand in mahjong is rather difficult compared to poker, both rulesets have dozens of house-rule yaku that either don't exist or aren't generally recognized in the real game. As a consequence of this, upgrades in Aotenjo are generally a lot less effective than they are in Balatro. Leveling up yaku is done through "element books" - each yaku has an element and you get three upgrades at once instead of picking one, except that unlike poker, you're generally going to stack multiple yaku at once and the ones that typically stack are usually in different packs. Likewise, tile removal isn't as effective when you have 136 tiles (or more on certain decks) lying around. Aotenjo's equivalent of jokers also tend to concentrate on suits and a lot of them rotate which suit they apply to, so you can't really pre-plan tile removal the way you can with a poker deck. Speaking of jokers, the "artifacts" in Aotenjo tend to be kind of terrible. Many of them have extremely specific activation conditions and don't provide enough of a benefit to justify how difficult they are to build around, and there are some that are outright useless as far as I can tell. The developer has gone through multiple balance passes on the artifacts and I don't know that they'll ever achieve balance. I don't know that I'd say avoid, but definitely know what you're in for.
